**Jodrell Bank Observatory** ( [_JOD-rəl_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key")) in [Cheshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheshire "Cheshire"), England, hosts a number of [radio telescopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_telescope "Radio telescope") as part of the [Jodrell Bank Centre for Astrophysics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jodrell_Bank_Centre_for_Astrophysics "Jodrell Bank Centre for Astrophysics") at the [University of Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Manchester "University of Manchester"). The [observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Observatory "Observatory") was established in 1945 by [Bernard Lovell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Lovell "Bernard Lovell"), a radio astronomer at the university, to investigate [cosmic rays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_ray "Cosmic ray") after his work on [radar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radar "Radar") in the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War"). It has since played an important role in the research of [meteoroids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meteoroid "Meteoroid"), [quasars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasar "Quasar"), [pulsars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulsar "Pulsar"), [masers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astrophysical_maser "Astrophysical maser"), and [gravitational lenses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravitational_lens "Gravitational lens"), and was heavily involved with the tracking of Soviet and US spacecraft of the [Space Race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Race "Space Race").

The main telescope at the observatory is the [Lovell Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lovell_Telescope "Lovell Telescope"). Its diameter of 250 ft (76 m) makes it the third largest steerable radio telescope in the world. There are three other active telescopes at the observatory; the [Mark II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_II_(radio_telescope) "Mark II (radio telescope)") and 42 ft (13 m) and 7 m diameter radio telescopes.

Jodrell Bank Observatory hosts the global headquarters of the [Square Kilometre Array](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_Kilometre_Array "Square Kilometre Array") and is the base of the [Multi-Element Radio Linked Interferometer Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MERLIN "MERLIN") (MERLIN), a National Facility run by the University of Manchester on behalf of the [Science and Technology Facilities Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_and_Technology_Facilities_Council "Science and Technology Facilities Council").

The Jodrell Bank Visitor Centre and an [arboretum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arboretum "Arboretum") are in [Lower Withington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Withington "Lower Withington"), and the Lovell Telescope and the observatory near [Goostrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goostrey "Goostrey") and [Holmes Chapel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holmes_Chapel "Holmes Chapel"). The observatory is reached from the [A535](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A535_road "A535 road"). The [Crewe to Manchester Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crewe_to_Manchester_Line "Crewe to Manchester Line") passes by the site, and [Goostrey station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goostrey_railway_station "Goostrey railway station") is a short distance away. In 2019, the observatory became a [UNESCO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO "UNESCO")[World Heritage Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jodrell_Bank_Observatory#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jodrell_Bank_Observatory#cite_note-2)

## Full Article

*   **Official nam**e: Jodrell Bank Observatory
*   **Location:** Cheshire County, England
*   **Type:** Cultural
*   **Year of inscription:** 2019

The _Jodrell Bank Observatory_ consists of a series of radio telescopes located in rural northwestern England. Jodrell Bank is one of the pioneering observatories in [radio astronomy](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/radio-astronomy), the science of studying the sky through radio waves. It was founded in 1945 to detect [cosmic rays](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/astronomy-and-astrophysics/cosmic-rays-composition-and-detection) and was briefly used as an early warning system for potential Soviet missile launches. In the early days of space exploration, its telescopes were among the few on Earth that could track spacecraft and were involved in monitoring the [first Moon landing](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/moon-landing-1960s) in 1969. Over the years, Jodrell Bank grew to become an indispensable tool in observing objects both within our solar system and the depths of space.

Jodrell Bank’s 2019 inclusion on the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) World Heritage list recognizes its status as one of the defining achievements in the history of radio astronomy. The observatory’s signature telescope is its largest, the 250-foot (76-meter) wide Lovell Telescope, named after the observatory’s founder, Sir Bernard Lovell. The telescope was the largest steerable radio telescope in the world at the time of its construction in 1957 and remained the third-largest of its kind into the 2020s.

### History

The science of using radio waves to detect distant objects developed during the early twentieth century and eventually evolved to become the radar systems used by both sides during [World War II](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/military-history-and-science/world-war-ii) (1939–1945). Bernard Lovell, a physicist at the University of Manchester in northwestern England, worked on aircraft radar systems during the war and believed the technology could prove useful in the field of astronomy. Lovell wanted to use radio waves to detect cosmic rays, high-energy charged particles from space that constantly impact Earth. His experiments at the University of Manchester were hampered by interference from the city’s electric tram cars, so in December 1945, he took his equipment out to a university-owned site in the English countryside. The site was known as Jodrell Bank, named after William Jauderell, a fourteenth-century English soldier and archer. Lovell did not detect evidence of cosmic rays, but he instead discovered several meteors, small rocky bodies that burn up in Earth’s atmosphere.

Lovell was soon joined by several other scientists at the site, which was originally named the Jodrell Bank Experimental Station. By 1947, they had built the Searchlight Aerial, a rotating radar array to search for meteors, and the 218-foot (66-meter) Transit Telescope, which detected radio waves from the [Andromeda Galaxy](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/astronomy-and-astrophysics/andromeda-galaxy)—the closest galaxy to the Milky Way. Although the early work at the site was a success, Lovell wanted to construct an even larger telescope that could be steered and pointed to any part of the sky. He worked with engineer Charles Husband to design a 250-foot (76-meter) radio telescope known as the Mark 1.

Work on the telescope began in 1952, but the project soon ran into several design roadblocks and was seriously over budget. The telescope was in jeopardy of losing funding and was only partially operational by October 1957, when the Soviet Union launched _Sputnik 1_ into orbit, the world’s first[artificial satellite](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/astronomy-and-astrophysics/jodrell-bank-observatory#). As the only telescope on Earth that could detect the missile launch that put the satellite into orbit, the Mark 1 suddenly became a priority for the British government. Within weeks, the telescope was fully operational. At the time, the Mark 1 was the largest radio telescope ever built. It remains the world’s third-largest steerable radio telescope into the mid-2020s. In 1987, the telescope was renamed the Lovell Telescope in honor of the observatory’s founder.

For the first six years of its operation, the Mark 1 also served as a secret early-warning system for Soviet missile launches. During the [Cuban Missile Crisis](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/cuban-missile-crisis) of 1962, the telescope remained focused in the direction of the Soviet Union for ten straight days. It was also used to track US and Soviet space launches throughout the 1960s. In 1966, scientists at Jodrell Bank were able to monitor the Soviet probe _Luna 9_, which [landed on the Moon’s surface](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/luna-9-makes-first-successful-lunar-soft-landing). In July 1969, the telescope helped track the [Apollo 11 mission](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/apollo-11), the first human landing on the Moon. When the lunar lander touched down on the Moon’s surface, Jodrell Bank was able to listen in to the astronauts’ transmissions.

However, Jodrell Bank’s true success was in its main purpose of studying the heavens. The telescopes at the facility played a role in the discovery of several milestones in astronomy during the twentieth century. They were instrumental in detecting cosmic background radiation, the “glow” left over from the universe’s creation in the [Big Bang](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/astronomy-and-astrophysics/big-bang). Observations at Jodrell Bank also played a large role in the [discovery of quasars](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/quasars-discovered), extremely powerful bursts of energy believed to be caused by supermassive black holes at the heart of young, distant galaxies.

Jodrell Bank still plays a major part in astronomical research into the twenty-first century. The Lovell Telescope has been upgraded several times since its construction and was still operational into the mid-2020s. The Lovell Telescope is one of four active telescopes at Jodrell Bank. The second largest, the Mark II, was built on the site of the Transit Telescope in 1964. The Mark II has a diameter of 125 feet by 83 feet (38 meters by 25 meters). The other telescopes at the observatory are 42 feet (13 meters) and 23 feet (7 meters).

In 2012, Jodrell Bank was named as the location of an office for the Square Kilometre Array, an international project that will construct the world’s largest radio telescope on two sites in South Africa and Australia. In 2019, it was made the project's headquarters. Jodrell’s Lovell and Mark II telescopes are also part of the Multi-Element Radio Linked Interferometer Network (MERLIN) that links together seven radio telescopes across England and Wales. Jodrell Bank is also part of the European Very Long Baseline Interferometry, participated in Cosmic Microwave Background studies, and, in 2022, opened the First Light Pavilion, a museum dedicated to its history and accomplishments.

### Significance

Prior to the 1930s, astronomers studied the sky primarily through optical telescopes, instruments that could only detect light in the visible band of the [electromagnetic spectrum](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/physics/electromagnetic-spectrum). During that decade, scientists realized that our Milky Way galaxy was emitting radio waves, a section of the electromagnetic spectrum with longer wavelengths and shorter frequencies. This allowed astronomers to view the universe in a whole new light and see what optical astronomy could not. The first telescopes at Jodrell Bank were built in the infancy of radio astronomy, and with the construction of the Lovell Telescope, the observatory became one of the most important sites in the emerging science. At the time of the telescope’s construction, Britain’s _New Scientist_ magazine called it the nation’s “greatest scientific instrument.”

The United Kingdom first submitted Jodrell Bank to UNESCO for consideration as a World Heritage Site in 2010. Nine years later, UNESCO announced that the observatory had made the list. UNESCO uses ten criteria to determine if a site warrants inclusion on the World Heritage list. To merit inclusion, a site must meet one of the criteria; Jodrell Bank met four.

The observatory is seen as “a masterpiece of human creative genius,” representing the entire history of radio astronomy from its infancy to modern day. The innovative telescopes designed by Lovell and his fellow scientists led to many ground-breaking discoveries and paved the way for further advancements. Similarly, Jodrell Bank meets another UNESCO criterion as an “important interchange of human values over a span of time and on a global scale.” This criterion recognizes the observatory’s position at the forefront of radio astronomy and the many contributions it has made during the past seventy-plus years.

The third UNESCO criterion met by Jodrell Bank is that the observatory represents technology that “illustrates a significant stage in human history,” specifically the period from the 1940s through the 1960s. This period marked the transitional boundary from purely optical astronomy to the use of radio waves, X-rays, and other forms of electromagnetic radiation in studying the universe. It also represented the era of “[big science](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/big-science),” when governments and universities began investing in large-scale, expensive scientific projects.

The fourth and final criterion declares that Jodrell Bank is directly “associated with events and ideas of outstanding universal significance.” This criterion is also tied to the observatory’s legacy as a pioneering structure in radio astronomy, but it focuses more on its role in introducing methods of astronomy that revolutionized the science and gave humans a better understanding of the universe.

Although the four active telescopes at Jodrell Bank still conduct important scientific research, they are also tourist attractions and receive thousands of visitors a year. UNESCO notes that many of the old, disused, or retired instruments and structures still exist in some form and are maintained and well-preserved into the 2020s. For example, while the Transit Telescope was replaced in the 1960s, parts of it remain on site. In addition, the surviving pieces of the Searchlight Aerial are preserved at the observatory as one of its protected structures.

One of my favorite haunts when young: the Jodrell Bank Observatory – part of the University of Manchester, where I earned my PhD in the astronomy department. Although it’s now used mainly for research in astrophysics, the largest instrument of the Observatory once played a significant role in tracking spacecraft. It's located on the Cheshire plain, in the north-west of England, about 9 miles from the town of Macclesfield.

The Mark I telescope, now known as the Lovell Telescope (shown here), was the world’s largest steerable dish radio telescope, 76.2 meters (250 ft) in diameter, when it was constructed in 1957; it’s now the third largest, after the Green Bank telescope in West Virginia and the Effelsberg telescope in Germany. Part of the gun turret mechanisms from the First World War battleships HMS Revenge and HMS Royal Sovereign were reused in the telescope’s motor system. The telescope became operational in mid-1957, in time for the launch of Sputnik 1, the world’s first artificial satellite. The telescope was the only one able to track Sputnik’s booster rocket by radar; first locating it just before midnight on 12 Oct. 1957, eight days after its launch. 

In the following years, the telescope tracked various space probes. Between 11 Mar. and 12 Jun. 1960, it tracked NASA’s Pioneer 5. It sent commands to the probe, including those to separate it from its carrier rocket and turn on its more powerful transmitter when the probe was eight million miles away. It received data from the probe – the only telescope in the world capable of doing so. In Feb. 1966, Jodrell Bank was asked by the Soviet Union to track its unmanned Moon lander Luna 9 and recorded on its facsimile transmission of photographs from the Moon's surface. The photos were sent to the British press and published before the Soviets made them public. 

In 1969, the Soviet Union's Luna 15 was also tracked. A recording of the moment when Jodrell Bank's scientists observed the mission was released on 3 Jul. 2009. 

Tracking space probes took a fraction of the Lovell telescope’s observing time, and the remainder was used for scientific observations including using radar to measure the distance to the Moon and to Venus; observations of astrophysical masers around star-forming regions and giant stars; observations of pulsars (including the discovery of millisecond pulsars and the first pulsar in a globular cluster); and observations of quasars and gravitational lenses.

The Lovell Telescope was the largest in the world when it was built in 1957

All scientific work carried out using the UK's largest telescope could end in the next two years.

[The government has decided to pull funding for the Jodrell Bank Observatory to focus investment on projects that deliver long-term impact](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5y6r9rdxygo).

It has left the University of Manchester, which owns the site in Cheshire, scrambling to find alternative cash before 2028.

Astronomers have described the move as "short-sighted" and a significant blow to the UK's research capabilities.

## Where is Jodrell Bank?

The observatory is a Unesco World Heritage Site and stands between two villages in the east of rural Cheshire on a site that spans less than one square mile.

It is dominated by the enormous Lovell Telescope and its 250ft (76m) wide dish, which can be seen 20 miles (32km) away in Manchester.

Across the campus, there are control rooms, the Mark II Radio Telescope and a visitor centre.

![Image 2: Getty Images The Lovell Telescope, part of the Jodrell Bank Centre for Astrophysics at the University of Manchester, near Holmes Chapel in Cheshire, north west England is pictured on April 30, 2008. ](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/919e/live/de56a8e0-8a64-11f1-b329-01e04c1ebb9b.jpg.webp)Getty Images

The rural Cheshire location was chosen as a quiet spot to listen to the stars 

The area of relatively flat countryside was chosen by pioneering astronomer Sir Bernard Lovell as the perfect place to build an observatory because of its quiet radio environment, far away from interference.

He moved equipment into the open fields there in 1945, turning the area into a University of Manchester research station.

## Why was it built?

Sir Bernard founded the observatory because he needed a quiet place to study radio signals from space.

Before radio astronomy was pioneered by people like Sir Bernard, most observatories used visible light to detect objects in space.

He later decided he needed a larger telescope to help researchers detect weaker signals from space, and the Lovell Telescope was conceived.

Created in an era before digital computing, the calculations for the cylindrical frame that held the huge dish alone took a year to complete.

![Image 3: PA Media Professor Sir Bernard Lovell (left), director of the radio astronomy station at Jodrell Bank, Cheshire, and John Taber, chief American scientist there, take a breather in the open air beside the 250ft wide bowl of Jodrell Bank"s radio telescope as the giant instrument tracks the path of the American moon rocket fired from Cape Canaveral, Florida.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/a404/live/403691b0-8a79-11f1-b7a2-89c39e80e970.png.webp)PA Media

Sir Bernard Lovell (left) was a pioneering radio astronomer 

Completed in 1957, the 3,200 tonne structure had to be redesigned during its creation to account for advancements in the field of astronomy and issues with funding, which led to parts from two decommissioned Royal Navy battleships being repurposed fro use in the project.

It was the largest radio telescope in the world, and unlike others at the time, it could be steered to follow objects across the sky.

In the next decade, the smaller Mark II telescope was built to work alongside the larger telescope to increase the observatory's capabilities.

## What does it do?

A radio telescope like the Lovell catches radio signals from distant stars, galaxies and planets in space, turning them into pictures and scientific data.

The size of the telescope allows it to detect signals that are extremely weak, while the other telescopes at the site help scientists paint a more detailed picture.

It can then connect with the UK's e-Merlin network, which includes five other telescopes - in the nearby Cheshire villages of Pickmere and Darnhall, the Shropshire village of Knockin, at the former RAF Defford airfield in Worcestershire and about 140 miles in Cambridge - to improve its capabilities even further.

The Lovell telescope is the leading instrument in a seven-telescope network

The observatory has been responsible for helping identify objects like supermassive black holes, discovering new galaxies and tracking spacecraft.

The e-Merlin networks research has helped shine a light on how planets and their parent stars form and how galaxies evolve.

## Why is there a campaign to save it?

The Lovell Telescope has been overtaken in size by larger radio telescopes, but has continuously been modernised and remains key to the UK's radio astronomy capability.

It supports thousands of scientists who use its research, and 28 jobs could be lost if alternative funding cannot be found for the site.

The cut by the UK Research and Innovation agency comes while construction of a new super radio telescope in South Africa and Australia called the Square Kilometre Array (SKA) is under way.

The smaller Mark II telescope works in tandem with the Lovell Telescope, previously referred to as Mark I 

It is set to start gathering data in five years, and by failing to back Jodrell Bank, the UK risks missing out on this scientific bonanza, according to Prof Philip Diamond, the former head of Jodrell Bank as well as the SKA organisation.

"It's removing the science capability which is essential for the long-term health of UK radio astronomy and the SKA," he said.

"So it would have a severe impact on the training and career of young researchers."

The Science and Technology Facilities Council is continuing to fund some of the activity at Jodrell Bank through investment in the SKA.

The **Lovell Telescope** ( [_LUV-əl_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key")) is a [radio telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_telescope "Radio telescope") at [Jodrell Bank Observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jodrell_Bank_Observatory "Jodrell Bank Observatory"), near [Goostrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goostrey "Goostrey"), [Cheshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheshire "Cheshire"), in the north-west of England. Completed in 1957, the telescope was the largest steerable dish radio telescope in the world at 76.2 metres (250 feet) in diameter;[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lovell_Telescope#cite_note-1) it is now the third-largest, after the US [Green Bank telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Bank_Telescope "Green Bank Telescope"), and German [Effelsberg telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effelsberg_100-m_Radio_Telescope "Effelsberg 100-m Radio Telescope").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lovell_Telescope#cite_note-spaceref_resurface-2)

Originally known as the "250 ft telescope" or the Radio Telescope at Jodrell Bank, it became the **Mark I telescope** from 1960 as future telescopes (the [Mark II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_II_(radio_telescope) "Mark II (radio telescope)"), [III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_III_(radio_telescope) "Mark III (radio telescope)"), and IV) began design.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lovell_Telescope#cite_note-jb_telescopes-3) It was renamed the Lovell Telescope in 1987 after Sir [Bernard Lovell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Lovell "Bernard Lovell"),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lovell_Telescope#cite_note-bbc_surface_reopened-4) and became a Grade I [listed building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Listed_building "Listed building") in 1988.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lovell_Telescope#cite_note-listed-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lovell_Telescope#cite_note-images-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lovell_Telescope#cite_note-7) The telescope forms part of the [MERLIN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MERLIN "MERLIN") and [European VLBI Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_VLBI_Network "European VLBI Network") arrays of radio telescopes.

The telescope was influential in the early detections of [extragalactic objects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extragalactic_astronomy "Extragalactic astronomy") including [quasars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasar "Quasar"), [astrophysical masers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astrophysical_maser "Astrophysical maser"), and [Einstein rings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein_ring "Einstein ring"). Soviet and US [probes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_probe "Space probe") of the [Space Race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Race "Space Race") were tracked en route to the [Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon "Moon"), [Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus "Venus"), and [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars "Mars"); in 1966 it received the first imagery from the Moon's surface taken by [Luna 9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luna_9 "Luna 9"). At a height of the [Cold War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War "Cold War") in 1962 and 1963, the telescope operated as an [early-warning radar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early-warning_radar "Early-warning radar") of the [four-minute warning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four-minute_warning "Four-minute warning") system for the Soviet [Strategic Rocket Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_Rocket_Forces "Strategic Rocket Forces").

Both Bernard Lovell and [Charles Husband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Husband "Charles Husband") were knighted for their roles in creating the telescope.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lovell_Telescope#cite_note-jodrellbank_history-8) In September 2006, the telescope won the BBC's online competition to find the UK's greatest "Unsung Landmark".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lovell_Telescope#cite_note-bbc_unsung-9)

The telescope is visible from [Manchester Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_Airport "Manchester Airport"), high-rise buildings in [Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester "Manchester") such as the [Beetham Tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beetham_Tower,_Manchester "Beetham Tower, Manchester"), and distant vantage points such as the [Pennines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennines "Pennines"), [Winter Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winter_Hill_(Lancashire) "Winter Hill (Lancashire)"), [Snowdonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snowdonia "Snowdonia"), [Beeston Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beeston_Castle "Beeston Castle"), and the [Peak District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_District "Peak District").

### Conception and construction of the Mark I

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lovell_Telescope&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Conception and construction of the Mark I")]

[Bernard Lovell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Lovell "Bernard Lovell") built the [Transit Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transit_Telescope "Transit Telescope") at Jodrell Bank in the late 1940s. This was a 218 ft (66 m)-diameter radio telescope that could only point directly upwards; the next logical step was to build a telescope that could look at all parts of the sky so that more sources could be observed, as well as for longer integration times. Although the Transit Telescope had been designed and constructed by the astronomers that used it, a fully steerable telescope would need to be professionally designed and constructed; the first challenge was to find an engineer willing to do the job. This turned out to be [Charles Husband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Husband "Charles Husband"), whom Lovell first met on 8 September 1949.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lovell_Telescope#cite_note-story_28-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lovell_Telescope#cite_note-astronomer_195-11)
